2022_289_board_self_evaluation_template_.paragraph: A blank self-evaluation instrument for the Troy School District Board of Education covering the 2021-2022 school year, developed from the concepts and language of Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan's text 'The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together.' Trustees rate both the board as a whole and themselves individually on each listed attribute using a four-point scale in which 4 signifies a foundational strength of the board and 1 a critical weakness. The form is organized around six areas identified by Campbell and Fullan as central to high-functioning school boards: Coherence, a Governance Mindset, Systems Thinking, Strategic Focus, Deep Learning, and Managing Manner. Completed ratings were to be brought to a board workshop to guide a constructive discussion, with each section also asking for one or two concrete improvement ideas for the next 12 months.
2022_289_board_self_evaluation_template_.page:
Purpose and Source
The Troy School District Board of Education Self-Evaluation for the 2021-2022 school year is a rating form developed from the concepts and language established by Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan in 'The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together.' Its stated purpose is for trustees to reflect on their performance as a board and as individuals over the past 12 months and to use that introspection to develop concrete actions for improving performance as a team over the next 12 months. Wherever possible the attribute language is pulled directly from the text.

Structure
Campbell and Fullan identified six key areas as central to high-functioning school boards across the US: Coherence, a Governance Mindset, Systems Thinking, Strategic Focus, Deep Learning, and Managing Manner. The form's numbered section headings order them as Section 1: Coherence (Individuals' Shared Depth of Understanding about the Nature of the Work); Section 2: Governance Mindset (Core Understanding of the Basic Principles of Governance); Section 3: Strategic Focus; Section 4: Systems Thinking; Section 5: Deep Learning; and Section 6: Managing Manner. Each section is followed by a prompt reading '1-2 Ideas for improving our performance in this area over the next 12 months.'

Rating Scale
Focusing only on experience over the past 12 months, respondents rate both the board as a whole and themselves on each attribute:

| Rating | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 4 | A foundational strength of this board |
| 3 | Generally good |
| 2 | Needs improvement |
| 1 | A critical weakness of this board |

At the end of each section a summary rating for the section as a whole is requested; the instructions state this does not need to be a mathematical average but is instead more of the respondent's 'gestalt' after thinking through the section as a whole.

Attribute Blocks
The rating grids each carry two columns, 'The Board' and 'Me,' and close with paired 'Section Summary/Gestalt Rating' lines. The blocks run 1 through 15 (individual trustee attributes on depth of understanding, emotional commitment, trust, confidentiality, and avoidance of single-issue agendas), 1 through 15 (board-level attributes on unity of purpose, cohesive teamwork, accountability, budget tracking, and constituent communication), 1 through 6 (strategic focus and avoidance of micro-management), 1 through 4 (systems thinking and unintended consequences), 1 through 9 (deep learning, preparation, school visits, and confidence in administration information), and 1 through 8 (modeling behavior, courtesy, listening, and treating each other with respect).

Process
Trustees were directed to assess the TSD Board and their own performance on each attribute, use that assessment to guide suggestions for the team's future improvement, express ideas in terms of positive, concrete actions or procedural changes, and have the completed form readily available at the board workshop where the ratings would serve as a guide for discussion. The copy in the board packet is the blank template; no ratings or written responses are recorded on it.
2022_289_board_self_evaluation_template_.verbose:
Overview
The Troy School District Board of Education Self-Evaluation for the 2021-2022 School Year is a structured rating instrument distributed to trustees ahead of a board workshop. The introduction states that the evaluation form was developed from the concepts and language established by Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan as set forth in their text 'The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together.' The stated purpose of the assessment is to reflect on performance as a board and as individual trustees over the past 12 months, and then to use that introspection to develop concrete actions for improving performance as a team over the next 12 months. The document circulated with the board materials is the blank template; no completed ratings, gestalt scores, or improvement ideas are filled in.

Six Key Areas
The introduction identifies six key areas that Campbell and Fullan found to be central to high-functioning school boards across the US: Coherence, a Governance Mindset, Systems Thinking, Strategic Focus, Deep Learning, and Managing Manner. The assessment is organized around those six areas with individual attributes that were identified in their research as key contributors to success in each area, and whenever possible the attribute language has been pulled directly from the text. The numbered section headings in the body of the form present the areas in a slightly different order: Section 1: Coherence (Individuals' Shared Depth of Understanding about the Nature of the Work); Section 2: Governance Mindset (Core Understanding of the Basic Principles of Governance); Section 3: Strategic Focus; Section 4: Systems Thinking; Section 5: Deep Learning; Section 6: Managing Manner. After each of the six section headings the form repeats the prompt '1-2 Ideas for improving our performance in this area over the next 12 months.'

Directions and Scale
Respondents are told to focus only on their experience over the past 12 months and to rate both the board as a whole and then themselves on each attribute. The scale is: 4, a foundational strength of this board; 3, generally good; 2, needs improvement; 1, a critical weakness of this board. At the end of each section a summary rating for the section as a whole is requested, and the directions specify that this does not need to be a mathematical average but is instead more of the respondent's 'gestalt' after thinking through the section as a whole. Finally, respondents are asked to brainstorm 1 or 2 concrete ways the board could improve in each area over the next 12 months, expressed in terms of positive, concrete actions or procedural changes that could be implemented. The immediate task set out in the introduction is to assess the TSD Board and one's own performance on each attribute and then use that assessment to guide suggestions for the team's future improvement; the board ratings on the form will also be used as a guide for a constructive discussion at the workshop, so trustees are told to have the form completed and readily available at that meeting.

Attribute Grid - Individual Trustee Coherence
The first rating grid carries the column headings 'The Board' and 'Me' and lists attributes numbered 1 through 15: as individuals, trustees have a depth of understanding about the nature of the work; individual trustees demonstrate an emotional commitment to the work of the district, that is, the board 'owns' the strategic vision rather than 'observes' it; individual trustees actively reinforce a culture of trust through action, reliability ('I keep my word') and competence ('I am skilled at follow-through'); trustees believe the motivations and inherent beliefs of other trustees are honorable, ethical, and honest; individual trustees maintain confidentiality rules relating to personnel and closed session content; trustees interact on a continuous basis, sorting out differences and arriving at a common understanding that guides and reflects the actions of the district; as individuals, trustees recognize and reinforce the intrinsic impact and power in trustees working together as a single board entity; individual trustees effectively reconcile their core values and beliefs with the development of the board's shared moral imperative and board strategic goals; individual trustees avoid representing specific constituencies, instead focusing on the district's systemwide purpose and work; individual trustees avoid single-issue agendas; trustees remain open to different priorities held by other trustees; as individuals, trustees show a willingness to compromise as long as a decision reinforces the board's unity of purpose; because the district is governed by policy, individual trustees avoid damaging the ability of the board to govern and the district to carry out its mission by abiding by policies even when they vote against a resolution and do not undermine the implementation of the board's policy; as individuals, trustees avoid intervening at the administrative level to solve a problem for constituents; and individual trustees believe the motivations and inherent beliefs of the administration are honorable, ethical, and honest. The block closes with paired 'Section Summary/Gestalt Rating' entries.

Attribute Grid - Board Governance Mindset
The second grid also runs 1 through 15 and addresses the board as a body: unity of purpose driven by a shared moral imperative, described as a relentless commitment to the learning of all students, no exceptions (all children will achieve, all children will have quality teachers, all children will be in a safe, healthy learning environment); acting as a cohesive, unified team working together to create a common vision rather than a collection of individuals each with his or her own agenda and vision voting on unrelated issues; striving for common ground even when there are deep differences and difficulties; rather than striving for group agreement, working to ensure enough interaction and adult learning that some differences are resolved, new shared meanings are achieved, and remaining differences are understood; moving forward to the next issue once votes are taken, leaving behind any discord or hurt feelings; avoiding surface politics (a narrow view preoccupied with single hot button issues) in favor of deeper governance (broad consideration of diverse views focused on unity of purpose); striving to 'lead from the middle' by interpreting state and federal policy, working laterally with other districts and regional entities, and liberating those below within the district to do the right work; keeping the focus of its energy on students and learning rather than administrative tasks; taking into account diverse views relative to implementation of new policies; building and maintaining a strong governance infrastructure; supporting staff and creating a positive organizational culture; holding the district organization accountable to the community it serves; tracking measurable outcomes that mark progress and attainment; actively tracking the district budget; and keeping constituents informed and up to date on the work of the district.

Attribute Grid - Strategic Focus
The third grid runs 1 through 6: approaching responsibilities with a clear focus on achieving desired strategic outcomes; limiting questions of district implementation tactics to scheduled oversight reviews or essential discussions so administrative issues do not supplant the strategic work of the board; board meeting agendas being more focused on educational and student issues than on administrative work; maintaining healthy accountability without micro-managing by intruding into the 'daily fray' of administrative or instructional roles; remaining focused on the 'what' of governance (steering the boat) versus the 'how' of management (rowing the boat); and staying focused on long-term strategic outcomes versus short-term tactical, administrative objectives.

Attribute Grid - Systems Thinking
The fourth grid runs 1 through 4: acting at a macro-level focused on connected, holistic solutions and allocation of scarce resources tied to the district's strategic plan, characterized as a wide-angle lens with strong peripheral vision rather than a telephoto lens with sharp focus on one issue; consistently taking a broad, systemic view of the district; stepping back from solving immediate problems in order to explore and understand broader patterns and interdependency of issues; and thinking about unintended consequences, including how decisions designed to assist one student population or one area of the district might negatively impact another part of the district.

Attribute Grid - Deep Learning
The fifth grid runs 1 through 9: the board striving to be a group of learners going outside its comfort zone to gain new understanding; individual trustees engaging in deep learning on major educational issues and challenges facing students; individual trustees coming to meetings fully prepared; setting policies that ensure students will develop global competencies and skills required for living in a complex, unpredictable world (character, citizenship, collaboration, communication, creativity, and critical thinking); driving deep learning within the district; having confidence in the quality and validity of information provided by the administration; completing regular, purposeful visits to schools; collectively discussing strategies for addressing credibility concerns within the district; and ensuring all information gathering by board trustees reinforces openness, teamwork, and trust.

Attribute Grid - Managing Manner
The sixth grid runs 1 through 8: consistently modeling behavior the board wants Troy kids to emulate; trustee behavior in meetings demonstrating patience, understanding, respect, common courtesy, and sense of humor; trustees recognizing that the impact of their public statements is all that matters and intent does not; listening to each other with ears, eyes, undivided attention, and heart, adopting an empathetic approach focused on an intent to understand; reserving judgment on each other; keeping positions focused on content rather than the behavior or style of other trustees; treating each other with respect; and not taking differences personally. As with every other block, it ends with two 'Section Summary/Gestalt Rating' lines, one for the board and one for the individual respondent.

2022_290_ia_letter_of_understanding_2022.paragraph: A Letter of Understanding between the International Academy consortium districts and their respective education associations setting terms and conditions of employment for teachers assigned to the International Academy, running from 2022 through June 30, 2025. The Academy is a grade nine through twelve school-of-choice program operating at multiple campuses; teachers remain employees of their home districts, are paid on the home district step and salary track, and receive an additional IA stipend set by home district, with Troy's listed at $3,400.00. The agreement also fixes a 190-day teacher work year, a $32 per hour curriculum rate for enrichment and substituting, a three-step grievance procedure ending in binding arbitration, and club and department chair stipends ranging from $575 to $3,000.
2022_290_ia_letter_of_understanding_2022.page:
Parties and Scope
The Letter of Understanding is entered between the Consortium Districts and the respective Education Associations to establish terms and conditions of employment for teachers employed by Bloomfield Hills Schools and assigned to the International Academy. The Academy is a consortium of public school districts that combined resources to provide a grade nine through twelve program operating as a school of choice for residents of the consortium districts at various locations. The parties agree to amend and add to the terms of the home school district collective bargaining agreement. The agreement runs from 2022 through June 30, 2025.

Employment Status
Teachers assigned to the Academy remain employees of the home school district and are not employees of the consortium. Staff are selected from qualified teacher applicants employed by the consortium districts, with the Academy administration determining qualifications; if a position cannot be filled that way, the Academy asks a consortium district to hire a qualified candidate. Vacancies are provided in electronic format to home districts. Tenure rests with the home district, and each teacher signs an acknowledgment to that effect.

Wages and Stipends
Required days are paid per the home district's step and salary track on the home district pay schedule. For 2022-2023 the IA stipend is paid in two installments, the first payroll in December and the last payroll in June; beginning in 2023-2024 it is folded into regular salary. Appendix A stipend rates, based on 190 teacher and 185 student days for 2022-23:

| District | Stipend |
| --- | --- |
| Avondale | $4,500.00 |
| Berkley | $4,200.00 |
| Birmingham | $3,400.00 |
| Bloomfield Hills | $3,100.00 |
| Clawson | $4,500.00 |
| Huron Valley | $4,500.00 |
| Lake Orion | $3,500.00 |
| Rochester | $3,500.00 |
| Royal Oak | $3,500.00 |
| Troy | $3,400.00 |
| Waterford | $4,500.00 |
| West Bloomfield | $4,200.00 |

Part-time teachers receive a prorated amount based on FTE. Optional enrichment and orientation activities are compensated at the $32 per hour curriculum rate, with a maximum of eight hours per day, forty hours per activity, and up to six principal-designated activities per campus compensated up to 64 hours.

Work Year and Schedule
For 2022-23 teachers work 190 days including 185 student days; for 2023-24 and 2024-25, 190 days including 186 student days. Each teacher receives one paid discretionary day, non-cumulative, scheduled no later than April 15 with no more than ten percent of staff off on any one day. The normal daily schedule is seven hours and fifty minutes on Monday and two other designated days and seven hours on Friday and one other day, with 270 minutes of instructional time, a thirty-minute duty-free lunch, and at least forty-five minutes of posted office hours after the student day. A full-time teacher teaches six of eight blocks over a two-day cycle.

Grievances and Committees
Grievances are filed with the IA principal within fifteen working days, advance to the Joint Steering Committee's three-member Grievance Committee, and may be taken by the Association only to binding arbitration under American Arbitration Association rules, with the losing party paying the arbitrator's fees. A joint Professional Development Committee meets at least once per semester. Appendix B sets club and supplemental pay by category, from $3,000 for music groups to $575 for other clubs.
2022_290_ia_letter_of_understanding_2022.verbose:
Parties, Purpose, and Duration
The International Academy Letter of Understanding is entered between the Consortium Districts and the respective Education Associations for the purpose of establishing terms and conditions of employment for teachers employed by Bloomfield Hills Schools and assigned to the International Academy. The Academy is described as a consortium of public school districts who have combined their resources to provide a grade nine through twelve program operating as a school of choice for residents of the consortium districts at various locations in the consortium districts. The parties agree to amend and add to the terms of the home school district collective bargaining agreement. The duration clause states the agreement will be in effect from a blank 2022 date through June 30, 2025. The table of contents lists sections on Duration; Selection of Personnel, Transfers, Terminations and Reduction in Force; Wage Issues; Supplemental Activities and Club Pay; Department Chairs; Work Year for Staff; Tenure; Grievance Procedure; Teaching Schedule; Academic Freedom; Professional Development Committee; and Other Issues, followed by a signature page and Appendices A through G.

Personnel Provisions
Teachers assigned to the Academy are not employees of the consortium; they remain employees of the home school district and are considered assigned to the International Academy. A home district may hire a teacher for the purpose of assigning that teacher to teach at the Academy, and such a teacher is the employee of the home district. Staff are selected from qualified teacher applicants employed by the consortium school districts, with the Academy's administration determining applicant qualifications; if a position cannot be filled in that manner, the Academy will ask a consortium district to hire a qualified candidate. Vacancies at the International Academy are provided in an electronic format to home districts. Nothing in the section prohibits a home district from terminating employment pursuant to its collective bargaining agreement, policies and procedures, applicable law, or the Michigan Teachers' Tenure Act. Tenure is with the home school district and not with the International Academy or any other consortium district, and each teacher signs an acknowledgment of that fact.

Wage Issues
Teachers are paid for required days according to the appropriate step and salary track of their home districts, with regular paychecks issued on the home district pay schedule. For required days and hours worked beyond the home district's regular work year and day, teachers receive the stipend rates in Appendix A. For the 2022-2023 school year the stipend is paid in two installments, the first payroll in December and the last payroll in June; beginning in 2023-2024 the total stipend is paid as part of regular salary commensurate with the bargained number of pays permitted in the home district contract. Stipends are paid when a teacher is on paid leave of absence commensurate with home district agreements.

Special Compensation and Enrichment
Teachers who plan or participate in optional enrichment and orientation activities outside the established school day or year are compensated at a $32 per hour curriculum rate, with payment no later than the second pay period following submission of required documentation. Participation is not required and the Academy is not required to use IA-assigned teachers for these services. Activities are submitted to the enrichment team for review and are subject to administrative approval, with written notice of any activity not approved and completion of a pre-enrichment payment agreement. Maximum payment per day is eight hours, and a seven hour and fifty minute day is paid as eight hours. Maximum payment for an activity is forty hours times the hourly amount, and at each campus the principal may designate up to six activities per year compensated up to 64 hours; the principal has discretion to increase hours based on the activity planned, with Foreign Language Immersion activities receiving priority. Maximum payment may include up to eight hours of preparation time. Activities on a teacher workday are paid the hourly amount for time beyond the regular workday, except that a maximum of four hours is paid for travel. Before the activity the principal determines in writing the number of staff compensated and the hours for each. Teachers supervising Extended Essay students beyond more than one of the campus average are compensated at the curriculum rate up to five hours per student, with the example given that if the campus average is 4.12 and the teacher is assigned 6 students, the language applies. Teacher Handbook language will state the official due date is not the end of the Extended Essay process.

Supplemental Activities and Club Pay
Teachers are compensated for each supplemental club, organization, or duty in accordance with Appendix B. Remuneration may be divided between co-sponsors with written approval of all sponsors and the principal. Teachers give written notification of interest in a club advisor role by September 15th, principals notify sponsors of stipend amounts in writing by the end of September, and clubs are paid before the end of the school year. Appendix B activities require prior approval of the principal; teachers may be assigned a club, organization, or duty, and certain activities, especially Category III, occur outside the workday. Applications for a new club advisor position are made no later than the second week of the school semester year, with the Labor Management Council determining new advisor compensation. A minimum of 12 students must actively participate in a club, and the sponsor of a full-time club must provide a meeting or activity a minimum of 18 hours during the school year; co-sponsors may share the stipend on a prorated basis.

Department Chairs
A Department Chair is selected from the teaching staff for each of the following departments: Literature, History, Math, Theory of Knowledge, Personal Project, French/German, Spanish, Chemistry, Physics, Biology, Economics, Art, Music, Physical Education/Health, and Counseling. Each department may bring forward a recommendation; administration is not obligated to select the recommended member but shall not make a final selection without first receiving and considering the recommendation. The term is three years. By May 1st of the last year of a chair's term, administration notifies the department in writing, including email, of a request for a recommendation, and the department has thirty calendar days to respond. If no recommendation is made and no member wishes to serve, the current chair's term may be extended year by year. Extended vacancies may be filled by an Interim Department Chair through the end of the school year. Chairs are paid per the Supplemental Pay list in Appendix B, and the job description is in the IA Teacher Handbook and Appendix F.

Work Year and Calendar
For 2022-23 teachers are required to work 190 days including 185 student days; for 2023-24 and 2024-25 teachers work 190 days including 186 student days. In each case one teacher workday is a conference compensation day when teachers are not required to report. The 2024-25 calendar was to be negotiated and mutually agreed before the end of the 2023-24 school year. Each teacher receives one paid discretionary day per year, which cannot be carried over, is scheduled first-come first-served with principal approval and no more than ten percent of staff on any one day, and must be scheduled no later than April 15. There are 186 instructional days plus scheduled enrichment and orientation days. Two early release days a year are inserted for Extended Essay, Internal and External Assessment, MYP and DP Curriculum Alignment, Approaches to Teaching and Learning coordination, and IB requirements. Teachers must attend Open House. Parent/Guardian/Teacher conferences are scheduled for two days in the fall and include one mid-day session and two evening sessions, with format discussed through the Labor Management Team. Teachers must attend professional development hours in the school calendar unless excused; those falling below the state recommended thirty hours of annual professional development are encouraged to find additional opportunities to avoid falling short of the 150 hours needed to renew certification. Additional required PD outside the bargained calendar is compensated at the curriculum rate or offset with time during the workday, at administration's discretion, excluding offsite IB training.

Grievance Procedure
A grievance is any claim by the constituent association units or a bargaining unit member of a violation, misinterpretation, or misapplication of the International Academy Agreement. Time limits are measured in regular IA working days and may be extended only with written consent. If management does not file a timely response the grievance is automatically granted; if the Association does not, it is considered abandoned. At Step One the grievance is presented in writing to the IA principal within fifteen working days of the occurrence or of awareness of it; the principal schedules a meeting within five work days and responds in writing within five work days of the meeting. At Step Two, within ten work days the grievant may present the grievance to the Joint Steering Committee's Grievance Committee, consisting of three representatives from the constituent districts with one from the grievant's home district; the committee meets within ten work days and responds within five work days. At Step Three only the Association may take the matter to binding arbitration, filing within twenty work days under American Arbitration Association rules, with the losing party paying the arbitrator's fees and expenses. The arbitrator has no power to alter, amend, add to, or subtract from the agreement, and the decision is final and binding. Grievants receive paid release time for arbitration hearings, and timelines are tolled if a grievance is filed under the wrong procedure.

Teaching Schedule
The normal daily schedule is seven hours and fifty minutes on Monday and two other designated days, and seven hours on Friday and one other designated day. Report and end times are flexible so long as a minimum of forty-five minutes of office hour availability follows the student day in the teacher's instructional space; the example given is a 7:30am report time with work until 3:20. Office hours must be publicly posted subject to principal approval. The normal schedule has 270 minutes of instructional time per day. In an eight block schedule over a two-day period, a normal full-time schedule is six instructional blocks out of eight. Block E is for music teachers only: a Block E course meeting 45-55 hours per year earns one semester of release time block, and 90-110 hours per year earns two semesters; if the schedule does not allow for five instructional blocks in one semester, the teacher is compensated one-sixteenth of salary for the additional instructional block. Homeroom or seminar is not intended to exceed an average of forty-five minutes weekly, with agendas provided at least twenty-four hours in advance. Every effort is made to provide preparation periods on C Day, Interdisciplinary Day, and outside evaluation days including IB Evaluation and AdvancED. Non-music teachers assigned five or more preparations per semester receive an extra planning period where possible or one-sixteenth of salary, with a Product Team counted as a preparation. There is a daily thirty-minute duty-free lunch. After school staff or professional development meetings should end by 3:30 pm, with no more than two required after school meetings a week and four a month, and notice provided by Thursday for the following week.

Academic Freedom, PD Committee, and Other Issues
The academic freedom clause commits the parties to educating young people in the democratic tradition, developing inquiring, knowledgeable, and caring students through intercultural understanding and respect, and encouraging responsible teaching within the framework of the IB curriculum and school policy. A joint Professional Development Committee is established with elected members from each party and a teacher lead faculty member serving jointly with the lead administrator; it establishes a building or tri-campus PD calendar coordinated with the bargained IA school calendar, issues a calendar and agenda for the first day of all staff PD before the end of the prior school year, develops a year-long plan within two weeks of the new school year, and meets at least once per semester. Teachers will not evaluate or supervise support staff, though department heads work with administration to supervise and evaluate graduate assistants. For school closings the International Academy functions as fiscal agent of that campus. Leave days follow the home district agreement while the IA calendar governs teacher and student days. Absences are reported to the Substitute Management System of the fiscal agent for the campus. Teachers who substitute for another Academy teacher are paid $32 per hour. Teachers receive a conference compensation day for fall parent-teacher conferences, bargained into the calendar as a teacher workday. The Administration and Association maintain the IA Mentoring Program, overseen by the Professional Development Committee, with mentor training, a data curtain to ensure confidentiality, building administrator assignment of mentor and mentee, good faith effort to match subject and building, placement of experienced teachers new to the IA in year two or three, and a mentor coordinator plus an assistant at each of the other two campuses. An IA Teacher Handbook is created and maintained by administration and teachers. The agreement is specific to the International Academy and does not establish precedent at any consortium district for added hours or days.

Signature Page and Appendices
The signature page states that the negotiators of both parties reached a Tentative Agreement on March 9, 2017 and that International Academy teachers ratified the Agreement on a blank date, with signature lines for the Education Association President and Executive Director and for the Board of Education Superintendent and President; actual signature pages are on file in the Human Resources Office of Bloomfield Hills Schools. Appendix A sets stipend rates based on 190 teacher and 185 student days for 2022-23: Avondale $4,500.00, Berkley $4,200.00, Birmingham $3,400.00, Bloomfield Hills $3,100.00, Clawson $4,500.00, Huron Valley $4,500.00, Lake Orion $3,500.00, Rochester $3,500.00, Royal Oak $3,500.00, Troy $3,400.00, Waterford $4,500.00, and West Bloomfield $4,200.00; all teachers are placed on the IA Stipend Schedule effective 2022-23 and remain there for the duration of the agreement, with part-time teachers prorated by FTE. Appendix B sets co- and extra-curricular pay: Category A (Music) $3,000 for Band, Choir, and Orchestra; Category B (Tri Campus Leadership) $2600 for English, Spanish, French/German, History, Economics, Chemistry, Physics, Biology, Mathematics, Art, Music, Personal Project, TOK, Counseling, and Health/PE; Category C $1700 for 12th grade Class Sponsor, Building Extended Essay Coordinator, HOSA, Forensic Lead, Science Olympiad Lead, Model UN Lead, Quiz Bowl, Theater Director, PD Committee Chair, and Graduation Planning; Category D $1200 for 11th, 10th, and 9th grade Class Sponsors, National Honors Society, Forensics Assistant, Science Olympiad Assistant, Model UN Assistant, Subject Area Honors Societies, Peer Corp, Honors Convocation, and Tri Campus Mentor/Mentee Committee Chair; and Category E $575 for Building Mentor/Mentee Committee Chair, Other Clubs, Teacher in Charge, Art Show, Olympics Coordinator, and Yearbook Advisor. Professional Development Committee members may request up to 10 hours of curriculum pay for work done outside the workday, and Summer Online Government pays $2000 per section for up to 30 students per section. Appendix C contains the 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 school calendars; Appendix D contains Okma, East, and West daily schedules; Appendix E covers the International Academy Guidance Counselor, allowing contract extension up to four days at per diem rate and attendance or supervision of up to eight events including Ninth Grade Welcome, College Panel Event, two IA Enrollment Nights, Freshman Welcome Night, Financial Aid Information Night, career or student health programs, and Middle School Outreach, plus organizing Honors Convocation, Graduation Planning, Career Day, junior college planning meetings with families, and Freshmen Orientation compensated at the curriculum rate. Appendix F is the Department Chair job description, covering department operations, MYP and DP implementation, horizontal and vertical articulation of IB components, pacing guidelines and a common assessment calendar, departmental goals, curriculum monitoring, personnel and section recommendations, Cabinet meeting attendance, purchase recommendations, inventory, parent communication, and oversight of IB deadlines for internal assessment scores, predicted grades, and eCoursework verification; it is marked as not part of the contract. Appendix G is the Mentor/Mentee Committee Chair job description, providing for one chairperson for the school, pre-approved by the principal and based on the number of mentees, responsible for agendas and minutes, attendance, reporting to the Associate Principal in charge of Professional Development and KALPA, and meeting annually with the committee to evaluate the past year and set goals; it is marked as not part of the Letter of Understanding.

2022_291_m111522bdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held November 15, 2022 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:02 p.m. and adjourned at 8:47 p.m. The board celebrated passage of the 2022 Bond Proposal, approved by Troy voters on November 8th with 60% of the vote, recognizing student volunteers, the CAPE committee, and departing trustees Steve Gottlieb and Elizabeth Hammond. Under Resolution 22-085 the board awarded the 2023 Roof Replacement Project to JD Candler and Butcher & Butcher Construction for a total of $996,024.75, payable from the Building Site and Sinking Funds.
2022_291_m111522bdmtg.page:
Meeting and Attendance
The regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education was held November 15, 2022 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. Also present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson, Superintendent Machesky, and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, and West. Approximately 35 members of the audience attended. The meeting adjourned at 8:47 p.m. Minutes were submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary.

Recognitions
The TSD Mission Moment honored student volunteers for the bond. On November 8th Troy voters supported the 2022 Bond Proposal, which passed with 60% of the vote. Students from the Superintendents Student Advisory Board, National Honor Society, and the Creative Guild received certificates of appreciation for volunteering at Troy Family Daze, creating videos, participating in podcasts, and taking photographs. The board also recognized members of CAPE (Citizens & Parents for Education), especially committee chairs Alison Hendry and Casey Colussi. Creative Content Producer Thomas Butcher presented the November Student Spotlight featuring Troy High School senior Anurag Komaragiri, who wrote a song and will launch his own album. Steve Gottlieb and Elizabeth Hammond, each completing a six-year term, were presented with engraved clocks.

Consent Agenda (22-084)
Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond, the board approved items A through D: minutes of the October 4, 2022 Board Workshop; minutes of the October 18, 2022 Board Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for September 2022; and rescheduling the January 3, 2023 Board Workshop to January 10, 2023. Yes: 7, No: 0. There were no additions and deletions, no public communication on agenda items, and no personnel items.

Call to Order and Attendance
The November 15, 2022 meeting of the Troy Board of Education was held at the Troy School District Services Building, located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, and West. There were approximately 35 members of the audience. The minutes are signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typing notation GH/jh.

TSD Mission Moment: Student Volunteers for Bond
The minutes record that on November 8th voters in Troy spoke resoundingly in support of the 2022 Bond Proposal, and that the bond measure passed with 60% of the vote, described as a testament to the faith residents have in the schools and the value they see in the education provided for the district's students. The board expressed gratitude for residents' confidence in the fiscal responsibility of the Board of Education and their trust in its stewardship of their investment. The board recognized students from the Superintendents Student Advisory Board, National Honor Society students, and students from the Creative Guild for their efforts in informing the community about the Troy School District Bond. These students volunteered personal time out of school to work at Troy Family Daze, created videos, participated in podcasts, or took photographs to illustrate the improvements possible with the Bond Proposal. Students called forward to receive a certificate of appreciation were Thejo Akkoor, Farrah Alaowad, Nurayda Albeez, Aanvi Arora, Mason Bui, Emma Chen, Allison Diebol, Manushree Ganta, Diya Gehlaut, Sreejani Kanuri, Andrew Kwon, Maya Lalik, Trisha Mallempudi, Tanvi Mandadi, Niyathi Manivannan, Riya Mathur, Neha Menon, Shreyas Nagireddy, George Perakis, Carly Perrino, Matilde Rabajoli, Tarun Rajesh, Akshitha Sahu, Aanya Shah, Alex Shamoun, Sharon Thomas, Nela Vugdalic, Marlien William, Ray Zhang, Srivatsav Bendi, Leah Cerulli, Ana Sofia Hernandez Gomez, Brianna Johnson, Sophia Keil, Jack Kelly, Anurag Komaragiri, Michelle Nartey, Sonia Puri, Katie Redmond, Anoush Rophael, Cassandra Wilson, Jeffery Wu, and Michael Zheng.

CAPE Committee Recognition
The minutes state that passage of the bond could not have come without the work of parents, community volunteers, teachers, staff, and administrators, and single out the committee of Citizens and Parents for Education, or CAPE, whose dedication and work both behind the scenes and in public forums was integral to the success of the 2022 Bond Proposal. The board recognized CAPE members for exemplary service to the Troy School District, especially Alison Hendry and Casey Colussi, who were chairs of the committee. Those listed were Dave Lambert, Allison Hendry, Casey Colussi, Roberto Cruz, Britney Pickett, Kelly Martin, Marianna Perakis, Kelli Howard, Jason Cody, Rose Cody, Lindsey Larivee, Nicole Reinkensmeyer, Michael Glass, Stacy Glass, Caty Baydoun, Rachel Preblich, Tony Sarna, Anthony Rosenblum, Michelle Phillips, Jeanette Eastburn, Nan Mueller, Kristin Kender, Carrie Leser, Holly Gordon, Sarah Philips, Andrea Debusschere, Amber Barbieri, Ayessa Potts, Shari Pawlus, Mandy Kostrzewski, Christine Wigman, Angie Lentner, Judy Bunao, Anne Sackrison, Matt Sackrison, Elizabeth Hammond, Scott Courtney, Anne Hallberg, Marti Steiner, Tony Lucchi, Betsy Murphy, Nancy Haboush, and Jason Cichowicz.

Student Spotlight
The board introduced Thomas Butcher, Troy School District Creative Content Producer, to share November's Student Spotlight, a recurring recognition in which students in the Creative Guild are featured each month to share their special accomplishments. Anurag Komaragiri, a senior from Troy High School, was recognized for creating a project that has provided opportunities for multiple Troy School District students. Thomas Butcher shared a song Anurag wrote himself; Anurag will be launching his own album soon.

Six Years of Service
Steve Gottlieb and Elizabeth Hammond will be leaving the Troy School District Board of Education after each serving a six-year term. The minutes note that in addition to being an elected position, serving on the Board of Education is a volunteer position requiring a great deal of time, effort, and commitment, and that Mr. Gottlieb and Mrs. Hammond have done a remarkable service to past and future generations of Troy students. Dr. Machesky, on behalf of the Troy School District, thanked them for their years of service to students, staff, and families. They were presented with a gift of a clock engraved with their name and years of service.

Additions and Deletions; Public Communication on Agenda Items
Both items are recorded as None.

General Consent Agenda - Resolution 22-084
It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A, B, C, and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the October 4, 2022 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the October 18, 2022 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report for September 2022; and rescheduling the January 3, 2023 Board Workshop to January 10, 2023. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

Personnel
Recorded as None.

Curriculum - Report: Academic Achievement Review
Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction Kris Griffor and Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction Christine DiPilato shared a PowerPoint presentation highlighting the academic achievement of students. They spoke about the green pillar and the importance of a high-quality preschool experience prior to entering kindergarten; the red pillar and ensuring a focus on equity and well-being with investment in supports to address the needs of all students; and the blue pillar objectives of creating and sustaining systems of support at all levels that deepen learning, together with the need to upgrade facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment. The 2022 fall assessment of student achievement was reviewed in detail, sharing proficiency charts and comparing data with surrounding districts. Gold pillar objectives were discussed along with professional learning opportunities for staff, community members, and students. There was some board discussion; the presentation had been provided in detail at the November 1st Board Workshop.

Business - 2023 Roof Replacement Project - Resolution 22-085
It was moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the bid roof replacement be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Funds. JD Candler was awarded Costello, Hill, and Operations at $526,200.00. Butcher & Butcher Construction was awarded Barnard, Bemis, and Wass at $422,395.00. Contingency was set at $47,429.75. The TOTAL stated is $996,024.75. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

Public Communication - Non-Agenda Items
Mr. Jeff Schaeper, Troy resident, addressed the board about curriculum and the ELA scores shared during the academic achievement presentation, offering constructive criticism and congratulating his opponents who won the election. Mr. Joe Thilman, Troy resident, addressed the board about racism in schools and how equity damages children, saying it should be about the quality of being fair and impartial, and that people need to become educated and more compassionate in schools about inclusiveness. Mrs. Amber Barbieri, TSD parent, asked the district to be equitable to 5th and 8th grade students at Troy Union and Smith, where the middle and high school paths are split between two different schools, and described how difficult it is on students to leave their friends at such an important time. Mr. Casey Colussi, TSD parent, thanked the parents of CAPE and Alison Hendry for leading the group, shared how proud he is of the community, thanked the administration for their efforts, and said Troy will become a destination city for its schools.

Reports from Student Representatives to the Board
Sara Ali, student representative for Athens High School, reported on events and activities at Athens. Nish Palepu, student representative for Troy High School, reported on events and activities at his school. Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East, reported on events and activities at her school. Alexi Papadelis, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, reported on events and activities at her school.

Board Member Comments
Dr. Philippart shared how proud she is to be part of the community and said she was happy to see the election results. She shared news of the passing of retired Troy Board member Ida Edmunds, noting that Edmunds was the longest serving board member in the state and an educational pillar in the community; a memorial service was planned for December 3rd at 10:00 a.m. at Desmond's Funeral Home in Troy. Mrs. Hammond thanked Kerry Birmingham and the administration for their work on the bond campaign. Mr. Gottlieb reported attending an ELA classroom that day where the discussion covered the Oakland University program on 6 C's NPDL, noting that TSD has already been doing that and commending the processes already in place. Mrs. Anne mentioned seeing the Descendants play at Athens and attending a STEM event at Saline High School on Saturday, and thanked the citizens of Troy for voting for the bond. Mr. Hauff wished everyone a heartfelt Thanksgiving. Dr. Wilson thanked the community and Central Office for their work on the bond, thanked Steve and Elizabeth for their commitment to the board, and mentioned the Descendants and Troy High's upcoming performance of Radium Girls. Dr. Machesky said he would attend the K-12 Alliance Executive Conference at the end of November in Washington, D.C. to work with legislators and advocate before the NSBA Advocacy Conference in January; he thanked everyone for their work on the bond proposal, thanked Alison Hendry for educating the community, thanked Kerry Birmingham for running the bond campaign, thanked Mr. Gottlieb and Mrs. Hammond for their years of service, and wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving. Mr. Schmidt thanked the community for voting for the bond, expressed pride in the Troy School District, thanked the administration for holding public meetings and being available for questions, thanked Mr. Gottlieb and Mrs. Hammond for their service, and welcomed Mrs. Alic and Mr. Haupt to the board. He announced that the next Board Workshop would be held December 6th at 6:00 p.m. at the Administration Building and the next regular Board Meeting on Tuesday, December 13th at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

Adjournment
The meeting adjourned at 8:47 p.m.
